name: Self-Driving Laboratories
title: Self-Driving Laboratories
answer: Self-driving laboratories are lab systems that close the loop between experiment design, robotic execution, measurement, and model update. They aim to speed up discovery in chemistry, materials science, biology, and formulation by letting software choose the next experiment rather than a human. The scope covers both the physical automation and the computational decision layer, including simulation and data management. They are sometimes called autonomous labs or materials acceleration platforms.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Self-driving laboratories are lab systems that close the loop between experiment design, robotic execution, measurement, and model update. They aim to speed up discovery in chemistry, materials science, biology, and formulation by letting software choose the next experiment rather than a human. The scope covers both the physical automation and the computational decision layer, including simulation and data management. They are sometimes called autonomous labs or materials acceleration platforms.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A self-driving laboratory runs on robotic liquid handlers, robotic arms, plate readers, spectrometers, chromatographs, and other instruments, all connected through scheduling and orchestration software. Compute may be local, on a cluster, or in the cloud, and it hosts machine learning models, surrogate models, and simulation codes. Data infrastructure stores raw measurements, metadata, and provenance so that each run can be traced. Safety systems, sensors, and interlocks are part of the platform, not add-ons.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done as an iterative loop. A model or optimizer proposes a batch of experiments, the scheduler dispatches them to available instruments, and the results are captured and cleaned. The model is retrained or updated, and the next batch is chosen, often using Bayesian optimization, active learning, or design of experiments. Humans set objectives, constraints, and stopping rules, and they review anomalies.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance records who or what proposed each experiment, which instrument ran it, and how the data were processed. Reproducibility depends on versioned code, instrument logs, and calibrated reference materials. Risks include silent hardware failures, data drift, unsafe chemical or biological combinations, and unclear ownership of generated data or inventions. Access control, audit trails, and human sign off for high risk runs are common controls.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward more standard interfaces between instruments and orchestration software, more use of simulation to pre screen experiments, and tighter integration with large language models for planning and documentation. Cloud labs and remote access are expanding who can run experiments, while standards for data and provenance are still maturing. The field is shifting from bespoke one off systems toward reusable platforms, though validation and cost remain practical limits. Progress will depend on reliable automation, clear records, and careful human oversight.
